doc.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004

title: How Fleck writes and chooses tunes for the band
summary: Fleck writes constantly and picks the tune that has an intangible something, either striking simplicity or interesting complexity. He then problem-solves how it fits the group.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: When you set about writing new compositions, does the fact that you had three or four fourth members affect the way you’re thinking about new work?

Not so much. Like I just write a lot. And I’m always screwing around with the banjo and stuff pops out and then I try to figure out what’s going to be good for the group. And a lot of times I just take what I think is the best song and what makes it the best song to me is hard to put my finger on but I’ll just have something and I’ll think well this is — there a bunch, I might have twenty things that I come up with, this one I think is special. It’s usually something about the melody or the chords that’s different enough to either be — it has to either be so simple and strong and striking in its simplicity that it’s better than the other simple tunes that I’ve written or that the other guys have or whatever, or it’s got to have a complexity that’s interesting but not necessarily offputting. Just I’m looking for a certain intangible something. But when I find it I know it. And I always believe — by the time I’ve brought a tune to the band, they may not know it but I’m usually deeply committed to it. And I’m just going to put it out there and sort of see what happens. But deep down I’m just going to start problem solving immediately and try to figure out, okay what’s not working, what is working, how can Jeff’s role be made better, is he dominating too much or is he — because a lot of times our fourth person is usually our melody player, which would usually be the leader in most bands.
